Early on I used to treat an objection like an exam question. Somebody says the price is too high and I would have three answers ready, and I would deliver all three, and the deal would die anyway. What I do now is much slower. I repeat what they said, in their words, and then I say the thing I think is actually going on, and I say it as a question. Something like, it sounds like the number is not the issue, it is that you would have to defend it to somebody who was not in this meeting. About half the time they say yes, that is exactly it, and then we are having a completely different conversation, which is the one that was going to decide it anyway. The other half they correct me, and that is just as useful, because now I know.

The thing I had to unlearn was the word must. In my language it is soft. You say it to a colleague and it sounds like a suggestion. I would sit in a meeting in English and say you must consider the audit risk, and I could see the temperature in the room change, and I had no idea why, because in my head I had said something perfectly friendly. A very kind counterpart told me eventually. He said, when you say must, it sounds like my boss talking. Try might. So now I say you might want to look at that before Thursday, and the strange thing is that people actually do it. The weaker word gets the stronger result, and it took me about four years to believe that.
